content: 1. In the Dominican Republic, healthcare providers believe that other cadres of healthcare workers could be trained to administer injections, as many already do for various health needs. However, it is crucial that physicians or other qualified providers remain available to address complex health issues, potential drug interactions, and risk reduction strategies. This is particularly important until a client is stabilized on CAB-LA, as physicians may need to dedicate more time to these patients compared to those on daily oral PrEP (e.g., every two months versus every three months). 2. In high-income countries, there is a need to expand the PrEP workforce, as PrEP services are currently offered only through other healthcare services. 3. In Zambia, where homosexuality is criminalized, the National AIDS program aligns PrEP services with WHO guidelines. Civil society organizations implement the program, referring clients back to clinics for prescriptions and management of complex health issues. 4. In Lebanon and the Eastern Mediterranean region, dependable financing is essential. Demand creation for PrEP cannot occur without certainty regarding service delivery, supply availability, and adequate staffing to meet demand. This is particularly challenging with injectable drugs. 5. With guaranteed funding in Lebanon, NGOs could train focal points to communicate with client populations and create demand for PrEP. 6. Lebanon could benefit from diverse service entry points for PrEP, such as outpatient clinics, maternal and child health services, STI clinics, and adolescent health services. These entry points could increase awareness among providers and create opportunities to engage at-risk clients. In Uganda, these service delivery channels are well-developed and could be adapted for new PrEP products. Task-shifting, with appropriate training, is also feasible. 7. In Uganda, public information campaigns need to improve to raise awareness and create demand for PrEP. Current information is limited and overly focused on MSM and transgender women. Campaigns should be more inclusive, particularly for women and biologically female individuals. 8. In Thailand and Nigeria, information campaigns are needed to address general fears of injections and medications, including anti-vaccine and anti-medication sentiments. 9. In Vietnam, stigma exists within certain key populations, where MSM are stigmatized by sex workers as being more promiscuous or at higher risk of HIV. 10. In Myanmar, promotion and advocacy will be necessary to overcome hesitancy in adopting new approaches to HIV prevention. 11. In Zimbabwe, skepticism about new products like CAB-LA must be addressed through creative knowledge-sharing initiatives to build public confidence. 12. In the USA, initiating CAB-LA for new patients would not be considered until a relationship is established through daily PrEP for six months. This ensures the client is reliable in returning every two months for injections. 13. In the USA, similar to challenges with injectable HIV treatment, candidates for CAB-LA must be vetted to ensure they can adhere to clinic visit schedules. This is problematic because those who might benefit most from CAB-LA are often those struggling with adherence and life challenges. The risk of resistance necessitates bringing these individuals back to the clinic and transitioning them to alternative treatments if needed. 14. In Scotland, more stringent tracking and follow-up systems will be required for CAB-LA clients compared to daily PrEP clients, as some fail to attend three-monthly visits. The risk of resistance is a significant concern. 15. In Australia and Scotland, better HIV testing methods, such as fourth-generation tests or better, are needed to ensure clients starting CAB-LA are HIV-negative. Many lowand middle-income countries still rely on third-generation tests, which could pose a barrier if nucleic acid testing (NAT) becomes the recommended standard. 16. In Thailand, PrEP will eventually be included under universal health coverage (UHC), and CAB-LA should also be included once approved by the Thai FDA. 17. In the USA, most providers believe CAB-LA would be difficult to deliver outside traditional clinic settings due to the reliance on physicians or nurses for administering injections and managing complex health issues. However, some providers in the USA, Myanmar, and Spain expressed more favorable views about community-based delivery. 18. In the USA, pharmacy-based delivery of CAB-LA is possible, as pharmacists are legally allowed to administer vaccines. However, practical implementation depends on factors such as staffing, scheduling, follow-up responsibilities, space allocation, and protected time for CAB-LA delivery. Some pharmacists are comfortable with this role, while others are not, citing competing priorities, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. 19. In Guatemala, national policies or norms restrict certain procedures to specific trained health professionals, creating tension between private sector services and government resistance to task-shifting for CAB-LA delivery in community-based settings. 20. In Lebanon and Myanmar, cultural contexts limit the acceptability of injections to being administered by physicians. However, some physicians are open to task-shifting for CAB-LA delivery, provided other constraints are addressed. 21. In the USA and Guatemala, CAB-LA could potentially be self-administered by individuals accustomed to self-injection for other health needs. However, laboratory tests and monitoring would still be required. 22. In Vietnam, telehealth for oral PrEP delivery (telePrEP) has been highly successful, with clients uploading test results and receiving prescriptions by mail. However, this model is not feasible for CAB-LA. 23. In Spain, CAB-LA delivery could be integrated into community-based HIV services, as demonstrated during the COVID-19 vaccination campaigns. This would increase access, provided storage and capacity for administering injections are available. 24. In Spain, CAB-LA delivery, like daily oral PrEP, could also serve as an opportunity for STI control and risk reduction counseling. 25. In the UK, remote pathways for CAB-LA delivery could be conceivable, such as self-sampling for lab testing and self-injection. However, challenges include high false positives, inadequately filled samples, and the high cost of processing dried blood spots. 26. Some changes in staffing and clinic setup may be necessary to deliver CAB-LA, but these adjustments are considered manageable.
